subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What name is given to the point within the Earth where an earthquake originates?
questions.explain: The focus is the point underground where the earthquake begins, while the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure and record the vibrations produced by an earthquake?
questions.explain: A seismometer (seismograph) detects and records the ground shaking caused by seismic waves.

questions.q: At a destructive (convergent) plate boundary, what typically happens to the denser oceanic plate?
options: It is subducted beneath the less dense continental plate
It is pushed upwards over the continental plate
It slides sideways past the continental plate
It splits apart to form new crust
questions.explain: At a destructive margin the denser oceanic plate sinks (subducts) beneath the lighter continental plate, melting to form magma.

questions.q: What is the name for a plate boundary where two plates move apart from each other?
questions.explain: At a constructive or divergent boundary plates move apart and new crust is formed as magma rises to fill the gap.

questions.q: A volcano has very gentle sloping sides and is built up from runny, free-flowing basaltic lava. What type of volcano is it most likely to be?
options: A cinder cone with viscous lava
questions.explain: Shield volcanoes are formed by runny basaltic lava that flows a long way, producing broad, gently sloping cones.

questions.q: A river's load is repeatedly thrown against the bed and banks, wearing them away. Which process of erosion is this?
questions.explain: Abrasion is when the load carried by the river scrapes and wears away the bed and banks; attrition is when load particles collide with each other.

questions.q: How is dissolved material transported by a river?
questions.explain: Dissolved minerals are carried invisibly in solution, whereas traction, saltation and suspension move solid particles.

questions.q: On a meander, where is erosion greatest and a river cliff most likely to form?
options: On the outer bank, where the current is fastest
On the inner bank, where the current is slowest
In the centre of the channel
questions.explain: The faster current on the outer bend erodes the bank to form a river cliff, while deposition on the slower inner bend forms a slip-off slope.

questions.q: A river's meander neck becomes so narrow that during a flood the river cuts across it, and deposition later seals off the old loop. What landform is created?
questions.explain: When the meander neck is breached and cut off, the abandoned loop becomes a crescent-shaped ox-bow lake.

questions.q: What feature is formed at the base of a waterfall by the force of the falling water?
questions.explain: The force of falling water erodes a deep plunge pool at the foot of the waterfall through hydraulic action and abrasion.

questions.q: Which type of wave has a strong backwash and generally removes material from a beach?
questions.explain: Destructive waves have a weak swash and strong backwash, so they drag material back down the beach and cause net erosion.

questions.q: Why does longshore drift move material along a coastline in a zig-zag pattern?
options: Swash pushes material up the beach at an angle, but backwash drags it straight back down
Backwash pushes material along the coast while swash removes it
Waves approach the beach at exactly 90 degrees to the shore
Tides carry material directly out to sea
questions.explain: Waves approach at an angle so the swash carries sediment diagonally up the beach, but gravity pulls the backwash straight down, moving material along the coast in zig-zags.

questions.q: In the sequence of coastal erosion on a headland, what landform is left when the roof of an arch collapses?
questions.explain: When the roof of an arch collapses it leaves an isolated pillar of rock called a stack, which may later be reduced to a stump.

questions.q: Longshore drift carries sediment along a coast, and where the coastline suddenly changes direction the material builds out into the sea with a curved end. What landform is this?
questions.explain: A spit is a long ridge of deposited material that extends out from the coast where the shoreline changes direction, often with a hooked end shaped by wind and waves.

questions.q: Why do constructive waves tend to build up beaches?
options: Their strong swash deposits more material than the weak backwash removes
Their strong backwash removes more material than the swash deposits
They only occur during storms with high energy
They break very frequently, over 12 times per minute
questions.explain: Constructive waves have a strong swash and weak backwash, so more sediment is carried up and left on the beach than is dragged back, building it up.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a Stevenson screen at a weather station?
options: To house thermometers so air temperature is measured accurately in the shade
To measure wind speed and direction
questions.explain: The white, louvred Stevenson screen shelters thermometers from direct sunlight and rain while allowing free air flow, giving accurate temperature readings.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure wind speed?
questions.explain: An anemometer, usually with rotating cups, measures wind speed; a wind vane shows wind direction.

questions.q: A student wants to find out how much water vapour is in the air (its humidity). Which instrument should they use?
options: A hygrometer (wet and dry bulb thermometer)
questions.explain: A hygrometer, often a wet and dry bulb thermometer, is used to measure the humidity of the air.

questions.q: Which set of climate characteristics best describes a tropical rainforest (equatorial) climate?
options: High temperatures all year with heavy rainfall in every month
Hot summers and very cold winters with little rain
High daytime temperatures but very low annual rainfall
Mild temperatures with a distinct wet and dry season
questions.explain: Equatorial rainforest climates have consistently high temperatures (around 27 degrees C) and heavy rainfall throughout the year with no real dry season.

questions.q: A plant growing in a hot desert has a long, deep root system and a thick, waxy stem. How do these features help it survive?
options: The deep roots reach underground water and the waxy stem stores water and reduces loss
The deep roots keep the plant cool and the waxy stem attracts rainfall
The deep roots absorb sunlight and the waxy stem carries out photosynthesis at night
The deep roots anchor it against strong winds and the waxy stem repels animals
questions.explain: Desert plants such as cacti have long roots to reach scarce water and thick, waxy stems that store water and cut down water loss in the dry, hot climate.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Geography (0460) syllabus; The Natural Environment
